name: Ad Hominem
description: Attacking your opponent's character or personal traits in an attempt to undermine their argument.
real_world_example: Dismissing a doctor's advice on healthy eating simply because the doctor is overweight.

name: Appeal to Authority
description: Asserting that a claim is true simply because a valid authority or expert on the issue said it was true, without any other supporting evidence.
real_world_example: Believing a new software architecture is perfect just because a famous engineer tweeted about it.

name: Appeal to Emotion
description: Manipulating an emotional response in place of a valid or compelling argument.
real_world_example: A politician arguing we must pass a bill 'for the sake of the children' without providing facts on how the bill actually helps.

name: Appeal to Ignorance
description: Arguing that a proposition must be true because it has not been proven false, or false because it has not been proven true.
real_world_example: Stating aliens must exist because no one has definitively proven that they don't.

name: Appeal to Nature
description: Arguing that because something is 'natural' it is therefore valid, justified, inevitable, good or ideal.
real_world_example: Claiming herbal medicine is inherently safer than synthesized pharmaceuticals because it comes from plants.

name: Bandwagon (Ad Populum)
description: Appealing to popularity or the fact that many people do something as an attempted form of validation.
real_world_example: Claiming a specific brand of truck is the best simply because it's the highest-selling vehicle in the country.

name: Begging the Question (Circular Reasoning)
description: A circular argument in which the conclusion is included in the premise.
real_world_example: Saying 'The code is bug-free because I wrote it perfectly.'

name: Burden of Proof
description: Asserting that the burden of proof lies not with the person making the claim, but with someone else to disprove.
real_world_example: Claiming there is a teapot orbiting the sun and demanding skeptics prove you wrong.

name: Equivocation
description: Using a double meaning or ambiguity of language to mislead or misrepresent the truth.
real_world_example: Saying 'The sign said fine for parking here, so I thought it was fine to park.'

name: False Cause (Post Hoc)
description: Presuming that a real or perceived relationship between things means that one is the cause of the other.
real_world_example: Noticing ice cream sales and shark attacks both increase in summer, and concluding eating ice cream causes shark attacks.

name: False Dilemma (Black-or-White)
description: Presenting two alternative states as the only possibilities, when in fact more possibilities exist.
real_world_example: Saying 'You are either with us, or against us.'

name: Gambler's Fallacy
description: Believing that 'runs' occur to statistically independent phenomena such as roulette wheel spins.
real_world_example: Believing that because a coin landed on heads five times in a row, it is 'due' to land on tails next.

name: Genetic Fallacy
description: Judging something good or bad on the basis of where it comes from, or from whom it comes.
real_world_example: Dismissing an environmental study's findings solely because it was funded by an oil company.

name: Hasty Generalization
description: Drawing a conclusion based on a small sample size, rather than looking at statistics that are much more in line with the typical or average situation.
real_world_example: Meeting one rude person from a city and concluding everyone in that city is rude.

name: Middle Ground
description: Claiming that a compromise, or middle point, between two extremes must be the truth.
real_world_example: One person says the sky is blue, another says it's yellow, and concluding the sky must be green.

name: No True Scotsman
description: Making what could be called an appeal to purity as a way to dismiss relevant criticisms or flaws of an argument.
real_world_example: Saying 'No true programmer uses Windows,' and when shown a great programmer who does, responding 'Well, no TRUE programmer.'

name: Personal Incredulity
description: Concluding that because something is difficult to understand, or one is unaware of how it works, it is therefore not true.
real_world_example: Not understanding how evolutionary biology works, and therefore concluding it must be entirely false.

name: Red Herring
description: Introducing an irrelevant topic into an argument to divert the attention of listeners or readers from the original issue.
real_world_example: When asked about missing a deadline, pivoting to talk about how hard you worked on a completely different project.

name: Slippery Slope
description: Asserting that if we allow A to happen, then Z will consequently happen too, therefore A should not happen.
real_world_example: Arguing that if we allow employees to wear jeans on Fridays, soon everyone will be coming to work in pajamas.

name: Straw Man
description: Misrepresenting, exaggerating, or fabricating someone's argument to make it easier to attack.
real_world_example: Person A says we should fund space exploration. Person B responds, 'So you want to bankrupt the country for little green men?'

name: Texas Sharpshooter
description: Cherry-picking data clusters to suit an argument, or finding a pattern to fit a presumption.
real_world_example: Pointing out that three successful tech founders dropped out of college, while ignoring the thousands of dropouts who failed.

name: Tu Quoque
description: Answering criticism with criticism; avoiding having to engage with criticism by turning it back on the accuser.
real_world_example: Responding to someone pointing out a flaw in your code by saying 'Well, your code had bugs in it last week.'
